question: What is Java and what does the motto 'Write Once, Run Anywhere' (WORA) mean?
keyPoints: Java is a high-level, class-based, object-oriented programming language designed for platform independence.
WORA means Java source code (.java) compiles into platform-independent bytecode (.class files).
The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) interprets and compiles bytecode into native machine instructions for specific operating systems.
Enables Java applications to run on any device with a compatible JVM installed.

question: Explain the differences between JDK, JRE, and JVM in the Java ecosystem.
keyPoints: JVM (Java Virtual Machine) is the abstract execution engine that executes Java bytecode.
JRE (Java Runtime Environment) includes the JVM plus runtime core libraries required to execute Java apps.
JDK (Java Development Kit) is the full development kit containing JRE plus development tools (javac compiler, jdb debugger, javadoc).
Developers need JDK to write code; end users need JRE (or bundled JVM) to run applications.

question: What are primitive data types in Java and how do wrapper classes work?
keyPoints: Java has 8 primitive data types: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, and boolean.
Primitives store raw values directly in memory with fixed memory sizes.
Wrapper classes (Integer, Double, Boolean, etc.) wrap primitive values inside objects.
Wrapper classes allow primitives to be used in generic Collections and utility methods.

question: What is Autoboxing and Unboxing in Java?
keyPoints: Autoboxing is the automatic conversion performed by the Java compiler from primitive types to wrapper objects (e.g. int to Integer).
Unboxing is the automatic conversion from wrapper objects back to primitive types (e.g. Integer to int).
Simplifies code when working with collections (e.g. list.add(5)).
Unboxing null wrapper objects throws NullPointerException at runtime.

question: Explain the four fundamental pillars of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) in Java.
keyPoints: Encapsulation: Bundling fields and methods into a single unit and restricting direct field access via access modifiers.
Abstraction: Hiding internal implementation details and exposing only essential interface features.
Inheritance: Allowing child classes to inherit attributes and behaviors from parent classes.
Polymorphism: Allowing objects to take multiple forms through method overloading and overriding.

question: What is the difference between a class and an object in Java?
keyPoints: A class is a blueprint or template defining fields (state) and methods (behavior).
An object is a concrete instance of a class allocated in memory using the new keyword.
A class is a logical entity; an object is a physical entity with memory allocation.
Multiple objects can be instantiated from a single class blueprint.

question: What are constructors in Java and how do default constructors differ from parameterized constructors?
keyPoints: Constructors are special methods invoked automatically during object creation to initialize fields.
They have the exact same name as the class and no return type (not even void).
If no constructor is defined, the Java compiler generates a no-argument default constructor.
Parameterized constructors accept custom arguments to initialize specific instance state.

question: What is the difference between Method Overloading and Method Overriding in Java polymorphism?
keyPoints: Overloading occurs within the same class when methods share names but have different parameter signatures (compile-time polymorphism).
Overriding occurs when a child class provides a specific implementation for a method declared in parent class (runtime polymorphism).
Overriding methods must match parent method name, parameter list, and return type exactly.
@Override annotation verifies overriding accuracy at compile time.

question: Explain Encapsulation in Java and how getters and setters with private fields enforce data hiding.
keyPoints: Encapsulation keeps class fields private (data hiding) to prevent unauthorized direct modification from outside code.
Exposes controlled public getter and setter methods to read and update field values.
Setters can include validation logic to reject invalid state transitions.
Improves code maintainability, security, and flexibility for internal refactoring.

question: What is Inheritance in Java and why does Java not support multiple inheritance with classes?
keyPoints: Inheritance allows a child class (subclass) to inherit fields and methods from a parent class (superclass) using extends.
Java does not support multiple class inheritance to avoid the Diamond Problem (ambiquity when inheriting conflicting methods from two parents).
Multiple inheritance behavior can be achieved safely using interfaces.
Promotes code reusability and hierarchical relationships.

question: What is an Abstract Class in Java and when should you use it over a concrete class?
keyPoints: An abstract class is declared with abstract keyword and cannot be instantiated directly using new.
Can contain both abstract methods (without body) and concrete methods (with implementation body).
Subclasses extending abstract classes MUST implement all inherited abstract methods.
Used to define common base templates and shared code across closely related subclasses.

question: What is an Interface in Java and how do default and static methods work (Java 8+)?
keyPoints: An interface defines a fully abstract contract specifying methods a class must implement.
A class can implement multiple interfaces (implements InterfaceA, InterfaceB).
Java 8 added default methods allowing interfaces to provide method implementations without breaking existing implementers.
Java 8 added static interface methods called directly on the interface type.

question: Explain the difference between == operator and .equals() method when comparing objects and Strings in Java.
keyPoints: The == operator compares reference memory addresses (identity) for objects.
The .equals() method compares content equality (value equivalence) when overridden.
For primitives, == compares actual raw values.
For Strings, 'hello' == 'hello' may evaluate true due to String Constant Pool, but string1.equals(string2) should always be used.

question: What is String immutability in Java and why is the String Constant Pool used?
keyPoints: Strings in Java are immutable; once a String object is created, its character contents cannot be changed.
Modifying a String creates a brand new String object in memory.
String Constant Pool in heap memory caches String literals to save memory across duplicate declarations.
Immutability guarantees thread safety, secure classloading, and safe hashcode caching in HashMaps.

question: Compare String, StringBuilder, and StringBuffer regarding mutability, performance, and thread safety.
keyPoints: String is immutable; string modifications allocate new objects in memory.
StringBuilder is mutable and un-synchronized, offering fast performance in single-threaded operations.
StringBuffer is mutable and synchronized, providing thread-safe operations in multi-threaded environments.
Use StringBuilder for sequential loops and string manipulations unless thread safety is required.

question: What is the final keyword in Java when applied to variables, methods, and classes?
keyPoints: final variable: Creates a constant whose value/reference cannot be changed after initialization.
final method: Prevents the method from being overridden by subclasses.
final class: Prevents the class from being extended / inherited (e.g. java.lang.String).
Improves security and design predictability.

question: What is the difference between Checked Exceptions and Unchecked (Runtime) Exceptions in Java?
keyPoints: Checked exceptions (extending Exception) are verified at compile time; compiler forces handling via try-catch or throws declaration (e.g. IOException, SQLException).
Unchecked exceptions (extending RuntimeException) occur at runtime; compiler does not force explicit handling (e.g. NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException).
Checked exceptions represent recoverable external conditions; unchecked exceptions represent programming errors.

question: How does try-with-resources work in Java 7+ and why is it preferred over traditional finally blocks for resource cleanup?
keyPoints: try-with-resources automatically closes resources (streams, connections, files) declared inside try(...) parenthesis.
Requires resources to implement java.lang.AutoCloseable or Closeable interface.
Eliminates boilerplate nested finally blocks and prevents resource leaks.
Handles suppressed exceptions cleanly when closing resources.

question: What is the Java Collections Framework and what are the primary interfaces (List, Set, Map, Queue)?
keyPoints: Java Collections Framework provides unified architecture for storing and manipulating groups of objects.
List: Ordered collection supporting duplicate elements (e.g. ArrayList, LinkedList).
Set: Unordered collection enforcing unique element constraints (e.g. HashSet, TreeSet).
Map: Key-value pair mapping with unique keys (e.g. HashMap, TreeMap).
Queue: First-In-First-Out data processing pipeline (e.g. PriorityQueue, ArrayDeque).

question: What is the difference between ArrayList and LinkedList regarding internal data structures and performance?
keyPoints: ArrayList is backed by a resizable dynamic array; provides fast O(1) random access by index.
LinkedList is backed by a doubly-linked list; provides fast O(1) insertion/deletion at ends but slow O(N) positional search.
ArrayList incurs expensive resizing array copies when capacity limits are hit.
ArrayList has better cache locality than LinkedList node memory allocations.

question: What is the difference between HashSet and TreeSet in Java?
keyPoints: HashSet is backed by a HashMap, offering O(1) performance without element ordering guarantees.
TreeSet is backed by a Red-Black Tree (NavigableMap), maintaining elements in natural or comparator sorted order with O(log N) operations.
HashSet allows one null element; TreeSet throws NullPointerException for null elements when using natural ordering.
Use HashSet for fast lookups; use TreeSet when sorted collection ordering is required.

question: How does HashMap work internally in Java (buckets, hash code, index calculation)?
keyPoints: HashMap stores data in an array of Node buckets using key.hashCode().
Index location is calculated using hash % capacity (bitwise (n - 1) & hash).
Hash collisions (different keys matching same bucket index) store entries in linked lists.
Retrieval uses hashCode() to locate bucket and equals() to find matching key-value node.

question: What are Generics in Java and how do they provide compile-time type safety?
keyPoints: Generics allow classes, interfaces, and methods to operate on parameterized types (e.g. List<String>).
Provides compile-time type checking, catching type mismatch errors during compilation.
Eliminates needing explicit manual type casting when retrieving items from collections.
Prevents runtime ClassCastException.

question: What is a Lambda Expression in Java 8 and what is a Functional Interface (@FunctionalInterface)?
keyPoints: A Lambda expression is an anonymous concise function representation ((params) -> expression).
A Functional Interface is an interface declared with exactly ONE abstract method (annotated with @FunctionalInterface).
Lambda expressions provide inline implementations for functional interfaces (e.g. Runnable, Comparator, Predicate).
Enables functional programming styles in Java.

question: What is the role of the static keyword in Java when applied to variables, methods, and nested classes?
keyPoints: static variables: Shared across all instances of a class, stored in JVM Metaspace/Class static memory.
static methods: Belong to the class itself, called without creating instances, cannot access non-static instance fields directly.
static nested class: Nested class that does not hold implicit reference to outer class instance.
static initialization blocks execute once when class is loaded into JVM.

question: How does JVM Memory Architecture divide memory into Heap, Stack, Metaspace, Program Counter, and Native Method Stacks?
keyPoints: Heap Memory: Shared across threads, stores all object instances and array allocations.
Stack Memory: Thread-private, stores primitive variables and stack frames for active method calls.
Metaspace: Out-of-heap native memory storing class metadata, method structures, and static variables (replaced PermGen in Java 8).
Program Counter (PC) Register: Tracks current JVM instruction execution per thread.

question: How does Garbage Collection work in Java? Compare Young Generation (Eden, Survivor) and Old Generation memory pools.
keyPoints: Generational GC assumes most objects die young.
Young Generation: New objects allocated in Eden space; surviving objects copied between Survivor spaces (S0/S1) during Minor GC.
Old (Tenured) Generation: Objects surviving multiple GC cycles are promoted to Old Gen, collected via Major/Full GC.
Minor GC is fast; Full GC scans entire heap and causes longer Stop-The-World (STW) pauses.

question: Explain Java Stream API operations: intermediate operations (filter, map, flatMap) vs terminal operations (collect, reduce).
keyPoints: Intermediate operations (filter, map, flatMap, sorted) return a new Stream and execute lazily.
Terminal operations (collect, reduce, forEach, findFirst) trigger stream pipeline evaluation and return concrete values.
flatMap flattens nested streams/collections into a single stream of elements.
Streams are consumed once and cannot be reused after terminal operation execution.

question: How does Multithreading work in Java? Compare Thread class vs Runnable vs Callable interfaces.
keyPoints: Extending Thread class limits single inheritance; implementing Runnable is preferred.
Runnable interface run() method cannot return values or throw checked exceptions.
Callable interface call() method returns a Future result and allows throwing checked exceptions.
ExecutorService submits Callable/Runnable tasks to thread pools for execution.

question: What is Thread Synchronization in Java and how does the synchronized keyword (Intrinsic Lock / Monitor) prevent race conditions?
keyPoints: Synchronization ensures only one thread executes a critical code section at a time.
synchronized method or block acquires the object's Intrinsic Lock (Monitor).
Other threads attempting to enter synchronized block are blocked in BLOCKED state until lock releases.
Prevents data corruption from race conditions in shared mutable state.

question: What is the volatile keyword in Java and how does it ensure thread visibility without mutual exclusion locks?
keyPoints: volatile guarantees CPU cache visibility: variable reads/writes go directly to main memory.
Prevents threads from caching stale variable values in CPU registers or L1/L2 caches.
Prevents instruction reordering for volatile reads/writes (happens-before relationship).
Does NOT guarantee atomicity for compound operations (e.g. count++ is not atomic).

question: Compare ConcurrentHashMap and Collections.synchronizedMap() regarding thread safety and concurrency performance.
keyPoints: Collections.synchronizedMap() locks the entire map on every operation, creating bottle-necks under high concurrency.
ConcurrentHashMap uses lock striping / CAS (Compare-And-Swap) operations for bucket-level fine-grained locking.
Reads in ConcurrentHashMap occur without locking, providing superior throughput.
ConcurrentHashMap does not allow null keys or null values.

question: Explain the Java Executor Framework (ExecutorService, ThreadPoolExecutor) and how fixed thread pools manage task queues.
keyPoints: ExecutorService decouples task submission from thread creation and lifecycle management.
Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n) maintains a pool of n worker threads processing a BlockingQueue.
Reuses worker threads, eliminating expensive thread creation and teardown overhead.
Rejection policies (AbortPolicy, CallerRunsPolicy) handle tasks submitted when queue and pool reach limits.

question: How does HashMap collision resolution work in Java 8 (converting linked list buckets to red-black trees)?
keyPoints: In Java 7, HashMap collisions stored entries in single linked lists with O(N) search time.
In Java 8, when a bucket exceeds TREEIFY_THRESHOLD (8 entries) and table capacity >= 64, the bucket converts to a Red-Black Tree.
Red-Black Tree improves worst-case lookup performance from O(N) down to O(log N).
Converts back to linked list if bucket size drops below UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD (6 entries).

question: What are Bounded Wildcards in Java Generics (? extends T vs ? super T) and the PECS rule?
keyPoints: PECS stands for Producer Extends, Consumer Super.
? extends T (Upper Bounded): Use when collection produces/reads elements of type T (covariance).
? super T (Lower Bounded): Use when collection consumes/writes elements of type T (contravariance).
Enforces safe compile-time generic collection polymorphism.

question: Explain the difference between Shallow Copy and Deep Copy in Java using Cloneable or Copy Constructors.
keyPoints: Shallow copy duplicates top-level primitives; referenced object fields still point to shared memory.
Deep copy recursively duplicates all nested objects, creating completely independent object graphs.
Object.clone() performs a shallow copy by default and requires implementing Cloneable interface.
Copy constructors or serialization are preferred over Object.clone() for deep copying.

question: How does CompletableFuture enable non-blocking asynchronous pipeline chaining in Java 8+?
keyPoints: CompletableFuture implements Future and CompletionStage interfaces for async programming.
thenApply(), thenAccept(), and thenCompose() chain async stages without blocking main threads.
exceptionally() and handle() provide clean asynchronous exception recovery.
CompletableFuture.allOf() coordinates execution of multiple parallel futures.

question: What are Java Annotations and how do custom runtime annotations (@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)) work via Reflection?
keyPoints: Annotations provide metadata information about code without altering execution logic.
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) retains annotation metadata in compiled bytecode for runtime access.
Java Reflection API inspects classes and methods at runtime to read annotation attributes.
Used extensively by frameworks like Spring and Hibernate for dependency injection and ORM mapping.

question: How do ReentrantLock and ReadWriteLock in java.util.concurrent.locks provide advanced concurrency features over synchronized blocks?
keyPoints: ReentrantLock offers tryLock() (timed lock attempts) and lockInterruptibly() to prevent deadlocks.
Supports Fair locking policy serving threads in first-come-first-served order.
ReadWriteLock separates read locks (shared concurrency) from write locks (exclusive access).
Requires explicit unlock() call in a finally block.

question: What is the Java Module System (JPMS / Project Jigsaw) and how does module-info.java enforce strong encapsulation?
keyPoints: Introduced in Java 9 to modularize the JDK and application packages.
module-info.java defines module dependencies (requires) and exported packages (exports).
Enforces strong encapsulation: unexported packages are inaccessible even via Reflection.
Reduces application memory footprint and enables custom lightweight JRE runtime images (via jlink).

question: Debugging Scenario: A high-throughput Java service experiences severe latency spikes due to Full GC pauses. Compare G1GC vs ZGC STW phases and tune JVM flags.
keyPoints: G1GC splits heap into region blocks, balancing pause time targets (-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200).
ZGC (Z Garbage Collector) uses colored pointers and load barriers to achieve sub-millisecond STW pause times on multi-terabyte heaps.
Diagnose latency using GC logs (-Xlog:gc*).
Tune heap bounds (-Xms, -Xmx) and Survivor ratios (-XX:SurvivingRatio) to minimize Old Gen promotions.

question: Deep Dive: How would you build a lock-free Bounded Blocking Queue from scratch using AtomicInteger and Compare-And-Swap (CAS) instructions?
keyPoints: Use array circular buffer with head and tail AtomicInteger position markers.
Use Compare-And-Swap (CAS) loop (compareAndSet) to atomically increment indices without synchronized locks.
Handle Queue Full / Queue Empty conditions using spin-waiting or LockSupport.park() / unpark().
Eliminates thread context switching overhead for high-concurrency message passing.

question: Architectural Design: How would you design a scalable financial transaction engine in Java ensuring ACID guarantees, idempotency, and concurrent updates?
keyPoints: Use Optimistic Locking (@Version) or explicit database SELECT FOR UPDATE row locking to prevent lost updates.
Enforce unique transaction idempotency keys to handle network retry duplicates safely.
Use Spring @Transactional with isolation level SERIALIZABLE or REPEATABLE_READ for critical account transfers.
Log double-entry audit trails to an append-only event stream.

question: Deep Dive into JVM Classloading: Explain Bootstrap, Extension, and Application ClassLoaders, and resolve ClassNotFoundException vs NoClassDefFoundError.
keyPoints: Classloading uses Parent Delegation Model: requests delegate up to Bootstrap -> Extension/Platform -> Application ClassLoader.
ClassNotFoundException occurs when class name is dynamically requested (Class.forName) but not found on classpath at runtime.
NoClassDefFoundError occurs when class was present during compilation but missing or failed static initialization at runtime.
Custom ClassLoaders enable plugin hot-swapping and class isolation.

question: Scenario: A Java app crashes with 'OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space' due to unclosed DB pools and static collection references. Diagnose using Eclipse Memory Analyzer (MAT).
keyPoints: Generate heap dump automatically on crash using -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=...
Load .hprof file into Eclipse Memory Analyzer (MAT).
Inspect Dominator Tree and Leak Suspects Report to locate accumulation point.
Follow shortest path to GC Roots to identify static variables or unclosed pool objects retaining unreachable memory.

question: How do Java 21 Virtual Threads (Project Loom) differ from traditional platform OS threads, and how do they eliminate thread pool exhaustion?
keyPoints: Platform threads map 1:1 to operating system kernel threads (heavy, ~1MB stack memory).
Virtual Threads (Java 21) are lightweight user-mode threads managed by JVM (~few hundred bytes stack).
When a Virtual Thread blocks on I/O, JVM unmounts it from its underlying carrier thread, executing other Virtual Threads.
Allows scaling to millions of concurrent threads without thread pool exhaustion.

question: Scenario: A deadlock occurs in a production Java service involving two threads acquiring nested locks in reverse order. Diagnose using jstack thread dumps.
keyPoints: Generate thread dump using jstack <pid> or jcmd <pid> Thread.print.
Inspect bottom of thread dump for 'Found one Java-level deadlock' block.
Trace Thread-1 holding LockA waiting for LockB, while Thread-2 holds LockB waiting for LockA.
Fix by enforcing a strict global lock acquisition ordering or using tryLock() with timeouts.

question: How does Method Inlining, Escape Analysis, and Scalar Replacement operate inside the JVM Just-In-Time (JIT C2) compiler?
keyPoints: Method Inlining replaces method calls with actual method body code, eliminating call frame overhead.
Escape Analysis analyzes if an object allocated inside a method escapes outside method scope.
If object does not escape, Scalar Replacement decomposes object into primitive variables on stack/registers without heap allocation.
Dramatically reduces GC pressure and speeds up execution loops.

question: Contrast Java Reflection performance overhead against MethodHandle and VarHandle for dynamic invocation.
keyPoints: Reflection performs security checks and boxing/unboxing on every call, incurring runtime performance penalties.
MethodHandle (Java 7) provides strongly-typed, directly executable references with JVM JIT inlining optimizations.
VarHandle (Java 9) replaces sun.misc.Unsafe, providing atomic and memory-fenced access to variables.
MethodHandle/VarHandle execute much faster than Reflection when invoked repeatedly.

question: Debugging Scenario: A multi-threaded cache experiences stale data updates due to Instruction Reordering and Memory Barriers. Explain the Java Memory Model (JMM) happens-before relationship.
keyPoints: JMM permits compilers and CPUs to reorder instructions for performance if single-thread execution is unchanged.
In multithreaded execution, reordering can cause thread reads to observe partially initialized objects or stale data.
Happens-before guarantees order: volatile writes, synchronized lock releases, and Thread.start() establish memory barriers.
Fix by declaring shared variables volatile or wrapping read/write accesses in synchronized/lock blocks.
